'''Margaret Scott Robinson''' (born 1951)<ref name=whoswho/> is a British molecular cell biologist, a professor and researcher in the [[Cambridge Biomedical Campus|Cambridge Institute for Medical Research]], at the [[University of Cambridge]].<ref name=frs/>

==Education==
Robinson received her [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in biology from [[Smith College]] in Massachusetts.<ref name=rnai>{{cite web|url=http://www.rnaiglobal.org/Member_List/Europe/Margaret_Robinson|title=Margaret Robinson|publisher=rnaiglobal.org|access-date=12 October 2013|archive-date=17 October 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131017093900/http://www.rnaiglobal.org/Member_List/Europe/Margaret_Robinson/}}</ref> She completed her PhD at [[Harvard University]] supervised by David Albertini and also [[Barbara Pearse]].<ref name=scottiephd>{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=Margaret Scott|last=Robinson |title=Endocytosis in granulosa cells |publisher=Harvard University |date=1982 |url=http://id.lib.harvard.edu/aleph/000695377/catalog  |oclc=9791498}}</ref><ref name=fancycoats>{{cite journal|last1=Sedwick|first1=Caitlin|title=Margaret Robinson: Vesicles wear fancy coats|journal=The Journal of Cell Biology|volume=206|issue=6|year=2014|pages=692–693|doi=10.1083/jcb.2066pi|pmid=25225335|pmc=4164944}}</ref> In 2003 she was appointed Professor of Molecular Cell Biology at the Cambridge Institute for Medical Research<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cam.ac.uk/research/news/professor-margaret-scott-robinson-elected-to-the-fellowship-of-the-royal-society|title=Professor Margaret Scott Robinson elected to the Fellowship of the Royal Society|last=|first=|date=26 April 2012|website=cam.ac.uk|publisher=|access-date=27 October 2016}}</ref> and is conducting research on [[Clathrin|coated vesicle proteins]].<ref name=rnai/>

Margaret Robinson was first exposed about science early in her life from reading about [[Marie Curie]]. While enrolled at [[Smith College]], she planned on being an English or theater major. However, due to university requirements, Margaret had to complete an introductory biology course. In that course, Jeanne Powell gave a lecture on cells and showed her students electron micrographs.<ref name=fancycoats/> This is when Margaret really became interested in cellular biology; the complexity of cells intrigued her.

After receiving her undergraduate degree, Robinson took a year off and ended up at [[Harvard Medical School]].<ref name=fancycoats/>
	
Robinson eventually joined a new lab and was able to conduct research on anything she liked. Due to her inexperience, her research did not go as planned and was nearly kicked out of graduate school.<ref name=fancycoats/> Robinson had to stop working on her interest in [[Clathrin|coated vesicles]] and work on something closer to what the lab was researching. 
	
Robinson eventually started a [[postdoctoral research]] with [[Barbara Pearse]],<ref name="fancycoats" /> joining her at the MRC [[MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology|Laboratory of Molecular Biology]] in December 1982.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Weston |first=Kathleen |title=Ahead of the Curve: Women Scientists at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology |publisher=MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology |year=2020 |isbn=978-1-903435-05-2 |editor-last=Stannard |editor-first=Dorothy |location=Cambridge, UK |page=107 |language=en}}</ref> Her interest was in [[Clathrin| clathrin-coated vesicles]] that binds to cargo. She eventually succeeded in purifying components of the coat that were not [[clathrin]] and are now known as [[Signal transducing adaptor protein|adaptor proteins]].<ref name=fancycoats/> These proteins sit between clathrin, which forms the vesicle's outer shell and also the vesicle membrane. Continuing, Margaret discovered that there were two different populations of [[Clathrin| clathrin-coated vesicles]], one that uses AP-2 at the plasma membrane and one that uses AP-1 and was associated with intracellular membranes.<ref name=fancycoats/> AP-1 and AP-2 are both heterotetramers with related subunits. They both have two large subunits and the other subunit is closely related in AP-1 and AP-2.

==Research==
Her achievements include the discovery of [[List of adaptins|adaptins]], which are specific proteins that manage cell-trafficking to ensure the correct cell cargo is transported to the right location.<ref name=frs/> She also discovered different combinations of adapting, when together with [[clathrin]], form a coat around vesicles that bud from intracellular membranes and act as transporters for protein packages to be distributed in the cell. She also developed the technique "knock sideways," which inactivates proteins in seconds.<ref name=cimr/>

After finishing her postdoc, she was able to start her own lab. Her main focus was to learn more about the [[Signal transducing adaptor protein|AP protein]] in depth.<ref name=fancycoats/> She had to also work with DNA because in order to characterize the complexes thoroughly, she needed to clone the subunits. Robinson and her lab managed to find another AP complex, [[AP3M1|AP-3]], which interacts with [[Membrane protein|lysosomal membrane proteins]] such as LAMP1.<ref name=fancycoats/> [[AP3M1|AP-3]] also interacts with [[tyrosinase]], which is a key enzyme in melanin biosynthesis, so [[AP3M1|AP-3]] is important for tyrosinase trafficking to premelanosomes.<ref name=fancycoats/> 
	
{{As of|2016}} Robinson has a lab at [[Cambridge Biomedical Campus|Cambridge Institute for Medical Research]].<ref name=cimr>{{cite web|url=https://www.cimr.cam.ac.uk/staff/professor-margaret-robinson-frs|title=Margaret Robinson: Cambridge Institute for Medical Research|date=4 September 2020 |publisher=cam.ac.uk|location=Cambridge}}</ref> She specifically works with coated vesicles. The best-characterized coated vesicles are the [[Clathrin| clathrin-coated vesicles (CCVs)]]. The coats on CCVs are primarily of [[clathrin]], [[Signal transducing adaptor protein|adaptor protein (AP) complexes]], and alternative adaptors. Her working hypothesis is that for each trafficking pathway, there are a number of different adaptors, each of which is recruited independently onto the appropriate membrane.<ref name=cimr/> Once on the membrane, the various adaptors would work together to package different types of cargo into the newly forming vesicle. Robinson and her researchers use several approaches to look for novel adaptors and other components of the trafficking machinery, including [[Proteomics|proteomic analyses]] of sub cellular fractions, [[RNA interference#Genome-scale screening|genome-wide siRNA library screening]],  [[Mutagenesis (molecular biology technique)|insertional mutagenesis]], and a new method they developed for rapidly inactivating proteins, called 'knock sideways'.<ref name=frs/> Her current projects include establishing the functions of AP-1 and other adaptors in differentiated cells; matching up machinery and cargo proteins; investigating how [[clathrin]] and adaptors are hijacked by the [[HIV| HIV-1-encoded protein Nef]]; determine why mutations in the non-clathrin adaptors [[AP4M1|AP-4]] and AP-5 cause [[hereditary spastic paraplegia]]; and exploring the evolution of adaptors.<ref name=spotlight>{{cite web|url=http://blog.wellcome.ac.uk/2014/07/14/researcher-spotlight-professor-margaret-robinson|title=Researcher Spotlight: Margaret Robinson|date=13 September 2023 |publisher=[[Wellcome Trust]]|location=London}}</ref> 
Her laboratory uses many techniques including immunolocalisation at the light and [[electron microscope]] levels, [[Cell fractionation|sub cellular fractionation]], [[protein purification]], [[proteomics]], [[Cytometry|flow cytometry]], [[live cell imaging]], and [[X-ray crystallography]].

===Impact of research===
Every form of eukaryotic life on earth contains [[Clathrin|coated vesicles]] and [[Signal transducing adaptor protein|adaptors]]. Her work is also speculated to play a key role in evolution of [[eukaryote]]s form [[prokaryote]]s over two billion years ago. Her work also has medical implications. Some [[Signal transducing adaptor protein|adaptors]] are mutated in certain [[genetic disorder]]s, and adaptors are frequently exploited by [[pathogen]]s . For example, the [[HIV]] genome encodes a protein called [[Nef (protein)|Nef]], which is required for the development of [[HIV/AIDS|AIDS]], and which works by hijacking adaptors and using them to modify the surface of the infected cell.
	
Robinson's work explains how coated vesicles sort cargo but also provides tools that can be used by others to address their own favorite problems. For instance, her newly developed method called knocksideways. Knocksideways gets rid of proteins rapidly. Her technique has found its way into other labs who are also interested in how particular proteins contribute to different stages of cell division.<ref name=spotlight/>

==Awards and honours==
Robinson has received many honors working as a cellular biologist. She was awarded a Wellcome Trust Principal Research Fellowship in 1999 and in 2003 she was appointed Professor of Molecular Cell Biology.<ref name=rnai/> She was elected a Fellow of the [[Academy of Medical Sciences, United Kingdom|Academy of Medical Sciences]] in 2001<ref>{{Cite web |title=Professor Margaret Robinson |url=https://acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/fellows-directory/ordinary-fellows/fellow/Margaret%20Scott-Robinson-0033z00002qIIXkAAO |access-date=2026-06-30 |website=The Academy of Medical Sciences |language=en}}</ref> and member of the [[European Molecular Biology Organization]] in the same year.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Margaret S. Robinson |url=https://people.embo.org/profile/margaret-s-robinson |access-date=2026-06-30 |website=European Molecular Biology Organization |language=en}}</ref> She was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS) in 2012.<ref name=frs>{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/margaret-robinson-12190|title=Margaret Robinson|publisher=[[Royal Society]]|location=London}}</ref> The [[Wellcome Trust]] also has funded her research for over 25 years.<ref name=spotlight/>
